hero.title: Access Control Models Explained
hero.desc: A practical guide to ACL, RBAC, ABAC, PBAC, DAC, and MAC — covering core concepts, trade-offs, analogies, and where each model fits best.

intro.p1: Access control sits at the center of every secure system. Whether you're building a document collaboration tool, a multi-tenant SaaS platform, or a high-security environment, the model you choose can shape your architecture for years.
intro.p2: This guide walks through six common models — ACL, RBAC, ABAC, PBAC, DAC, and MAC — explaining what each one does well, where it falls short, and when to use it.

acl.heading: 01 / ACL — Access Control List
acl.fullName: Access Control List · 访问控制列表
acl.title: The Per-Resource Whitelist

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Each resource keeps an explicit list of who is allowed to access it. Think of it as a guest list taped to the door of a private event.

acl.analogy: A whitelist posted on a meeting room door — only listed individuals may enter.

cons.1: Fragmented and hard to manage at scale

acl.scenario: Document systems, collaboration platforms (Notion, Trello), any scenario where permissions are resource-specific.

rbac.heading: 02 / RBAC — Role-Based Access Control
rbac.fullName: Role-Based Access Control · 基于角色的访问控制
rbac.title: The Organizational Model

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Permissions are assigned to roles, and users inherit permissions through the roles they hold. This is the model many enterprise systems eventually grow into.

rbac.analogy: Employees gain access based on their job title — managers, staff, and guests each get a different set of keys.

pros.1: Clean structure, easy to reason about

rbac.scenario: Enterprise back-office systems, HR/ERP/CMS systems, any organization with stable role definitions.

abac.heading: 03 / ABAC — Attribute-Based Access Control
abac.fullName: Attribute-Based Access Control · 基于属性的访问控制
abac.title: The Context-Aware Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Access decisions are evaluated dynamically based on attributes of the user, the resource, and the environment. This enables fine-grained, context-sensitive authorization.

abac.analogy: Allow access if: department = Finance AND resource = Report AND time < 18:00.

cons.1: Complex to configure and reason about
cons.2: Policies can be difficult to test and debug

abac.scenario: Multi-tenant SaaS platforms, conditional access systems, scenarios requiring dynamic, attribute-driven decisions.

pbac.heading: 04 / PBAC — Policy-Based Access Control
pbac.fullName: Policy-Based Access Control · 基于策略的访问控制
pbac.title: The Centralized Policy Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: Access control is governed by centrally managed, reusable policy rules — often written in a dedicated policy language. This enables auditability and consistent enforcement across systems.

pbac.analogy: Like an organization's internal policy handbook — every action must be justified by a written rule.

pros.2: Integrates well with OPA, Casbin, and other policy engines

pbac.scenario: Zero-trust architectures, multi-tenant systems, and compliance platforms — anywhere centralized policy governance is required.

dac.heading: 05 / DAC — Discretionary Access Control
dac.fullName: Discretionary Access Control · 自主访问控制
dac.title: The Owner-Driven Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: The owner of a resource decides who can access it, at their own discretion. This is the model behind file permissions in operating systems and sharing features in collaboration tools.

dac.analogy: The file owner sets "who can open this file" — just like sharing a Google Doc with specific people.

pros.2: Flexible and easy to grant access

dac.scenario: File sharing systems, OS file permissions (Linux), any scenario where resource owners should control access.

mac.heading: 06 / MAC — Mandatory Access Control
mac.fullName: Mandatory Access Control · 强制访问控制
mac.title: The Security-First Approach

core.title: Core Concept
core.desc: The system enforces access based on security labels assigned to both users and resources — users cannot override these rules. This is the model used in high-security environments.

mac.analogy: A "Top Secret" document can only be accessed by people with the matching clearance level — no exceptions.
mac.scenario: Military/government systems, financial core platforms — anywhere maximum security is the priority.

hybrid.heading: Hybrid Patterns: Mixing Models in Practice
hybrid.intro: In real-world engineering, no single model fits all requirements. The most effective systems layer multiple models to balance structure, flexibility, and security.
hybrid.pattern1: Role-based structure for most access, with fine-grained per-resource overrides via ACL. Common in document management and collaboration tools.
hybrid.pattern2: Roles define baseline permissions; attributes enforce dynamic, context-sensitive restrictions on top. Ideal for SaaS platforms with varying tenant rules.
hybrid.pattern3: Enterprise-grade combination for large platforms, zero-trust architectures, or multi-tenant systems requiring full auditability and policy governance.

decision.heading: How to Choose: A Decision Guide
decision.intro: Still not sure which model fits your system? Answer these questions to narrow it down:
decision.q1: Are your user roles stable and clearly defined across the system?
decision.q2: Do different resources need different access rules (per-file, per-record)?
decision.q3: Do you need dynamic, context-sensitive access (time, location, device)?
decision.q4: Do you need centralized, auditable policies for compliance or zero-trust?
decision.q5: Should individual resource owners control their own sharing and access?
decision.q6: Is security the top priority, even at the cost of flexibility?

access-control-models.conclusion: Access control is never one-size-fits-all. Strong systems start with a clear understanding of their security requirements, user workflows, and growth trajectory — then choose the model, or combination of models, that fits. If you're designing a new system, map out your access patterns before writing a single line of authorization code. Your future self will thank you.

hero.title: Launching a Personal Portal
hero.desc: Why I decided to build a personal website from scratch, and the design decisions that shaped it.

intro.p1: Every developer eventually asks themselves: should I build a personal website? The answer is almost always yes — but the follow-up question is harder: how?
intro.p2: There are countless options. Static site generators like Hugo, Jekyll, or Astro. Full frameworks like Next.js or Nuxt. Managed platforms like Notion, Super, or Hashnode. Each has trade-offs, and each pushes you toward a particular set of decisions.

vanilla.heading: The Case for Vanilla
vanilla.intro: This site is built with plain HTML, CSS, and a small amount of vanilla JavaScript. No build step, no node_modules, no configuration files. Here's why:
vanilla.point1: Simplicity — Every page is a self-contained HTML file. There's no extra mental model beyond "edit a file, refresh the browser."
vanilla.point2: Portability — The entire site can be deployed by copying a folder to any web server. Nginx, Caddy, Apache, S3, GitHub Pages — anything that serves static files.
vanilla.point3: Longevity — HTML is remarkably durable. There are no dependency updates, no breaking changes, and no "this worked last week" surprises. The site should work in 10 years much like it does today.
vanilla.point4: Performance — Zero JavaScript frameworks means no framework runtime overhead. The entire site loads in milliseconds.

design.heading: Finding a Design Language
design.p1: The hardest part of building a personal site isn't the code — it's the design. I discovered the awesome-design-md collection, which provides ready-to-use design systems extracted from real websites in the DESIGN.md format.
design.p2: I chose a design system inspired by Vercel's visual language, which emphasizes:
design.point1: Shadow-as-border — Using box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.08) instead of CSS borders, creating softer, more refined edges
design.point2: Bold letter-spacing — Negative tracking at display sizes (-2.4px at 48px) creates a compressed, engineered feel
design.point3: Three-weight type system — 400 for reading, 500 for interaction, 600 for headings. No more, no less.
design.point4: Achromatic palette — Grays from #171717 to #ffffff form the foundation, with accent colors used sparingly and functionally

structure.heading: Structure That Scales
structure.p1: The portal uses a flat, directory-based URL structure where each page lives in its own folder with an index.html. This gives clean URLs (/about/ instead of /about.html) and makes the hierarchy self-documenting.
structure.p2: Adding a new page is simple:
structure.step2: Copy any existing page as a template
structure.step4: Add a link in the parent list page
structure.p3: No build step, no frontmatter, no routing config. Just files in folders.

darkmode.heading: Dark Mode Done Right
darkmode.p1: The theme system uses CSS custom properties with a data-theme attribute on the <html> element. All colors, shadows, and surfaces are defined as variables that swap when the theme changes. The preference respects the OS setting on first visit and persists in localStorage after manual toggle.

next.heading: What's Next
next.p1: This is just the beginning. The portal is designed to grow incrementally — new projects, posts, and sections can be added without touching existing code. Some ideas for the future:
next.idea2: Search functionality with a lightweight client-side index
next.idea4: A /uses page documenting my tools and setup

launching-a-personal-portal.quote: "The best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago. The second best time is now."
launching-a-personal-portal.outro: If you've been putting off building your own corner of the internet — start today. It doesn't have to be complex. It just has to be yours.

hero.title: Personal Portal
hero.desc: The architecture and design decisions behind this website.

overview.heading: Overview
overview.p1: This portal is a static, hand-crafted personal website designed to run on almost any lightweight server. No build tools, no JavaScript frameworks — just vanilla HTML, CSS, and a little JS for theme switching and scroll animations.
overview.p2: The design system is inspired by the awesome-design-md collection, specifically Vercel's visual language: shadow-as-border, bold negative letter-spacing, an achromatic palette with functional accent colors, and a multi-layer shadow system for depth.

structure.heading: Site Structure
structure.intro: The portal follows a clean, flat URL structure:

zeroDeps.title: 📦 Zero Dependencies
zeroDeps.desc: No npm, no webpack, no React. Every page is a self-contained HTML file that links to shared CSS and JS. Deployment is immediate: copy the folder to any static server (Nginx, Caddy, GitHub Pages, S3, etc.).

designMd.title: 🎨 DESIGN.md Driven
designMd.desc: The visual language follows the DESIGN.md format from Google Stitch / awesome-design-md. All tokens (colors, spacing, shadows, typography) are defined as CSS custom properties in a single file, making the design system easy to modify and maintain.

darkMode.title: 🌓 Dark Mode
darkMode.desc: Theme switching is handled via a data-theme attribute on the root element, with CSS custom properties swapping colors. Preference is persisted in localStorage and respects the system's prefers-color-scheme.

responsive.title: 📱 Responsive
responsive.desc: Every page uses CSS Grid and Flexbox with fluid sizing. A single breakpoint at 768px handles the mobile ↔ desktop transition, with a mobile nav overlay for smaller screens.

a11y.title: ♿ Accessibility
a11y.desc: Semantic HTML throughout (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>), ARIA labels on interactive elements, keyboard navigation, and support for prefers-reduced-motion.

extensible.title: 🔗 Extensible
extensible.desc: Adding a new page is as simple as creating a new folder with an index.html, linking the shared CSS/JS, and adding a nav entry. No build step, no config files. The flat URL structure means clean permalinks out of the box.

deploy.heading: Deployment
deploy.desc: Copy the my-space/ directory to your server's web root. For Nginx, point the root to the folder and ensure index.html is served for directory requests. That's it.

hero.title: AI Explainer
hero.desc: Making complex AI concepts easier to understand through clear visuals and plain language — an interactive learning experience.

what.heading: What is AI Explainer?
what.p1: AI Explainer grew out of a simple goal: make artificial intelligence understandable for more people, not just engineers and researchers. It takes complex ideas like neural networks, transformer architectures, and reinforcement learning, then breaks them into visual explanations that are easier to digest.

why.heading: Why this matters
why.p1: AI is reshaping every industry, yet most people still experience it as a black box. Understanding the basics of how AI works supports better decisions, reduces unnecessary fear, and encourages more thoughtful use of these powerful tools.

ai-explainer.quote: "The best way to predict the future is to understand the present."

demo.heading: 🧠 Explore Core Concepts
demo.intro: Click on any concept below to learn more. These are the building blocks of modern AI.

nn.title: Neural Networks
nn.short: Computing systems loosely inspired by biological brains.
nn.detail: Neural networks consist of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons). Each connection has a weight that adjusts during training. Data flows through input layers, gets transformed by hidden layers, and produces output. Deep learning uses networks with many hidden layers to learn increasingly abstract representations.

tx.title: Transformers
tx.short: The architecture behind ChatGPT and modern LLMs.
tx.detail: Transformers use a mechanism called self-attention to weigh the importance of different parts of the input. Unlike earlier sequence models, they can process all positions simultaneously, making them highly parallelizable and effective at capturing long-range dependencies in data.

sl.title: Supervised Learning
sl.short: Teaching machines by showing labeled examples.
sl.detail: In supervised learning, the model learns from labeled training data — pairs of inputs and correct outputs. The model learns to map inputs to outputs by minimizing prediction errors. Common tasks include classification (spam detection) and regression (price prediction).

rl.title: Reinforcement Learning
rl.short: Learning through trial, error, and rewards.
rl.detail: Reinforcement learning agents learn by interacting with an environment, receiving rewards or penalties for actions. Over time, they learn policies that maximize cumulative rewards. This approach powered breakthroughs like AlphaGo and is used in robotics, game AI, and RLHF for LLM alignment.

nlp.title: Natural Language Processing
nlp.short: How machines understand and generate human language.
nlp.detail: NLP encompasses tasks like text classification, translation, summarization, and question-answering. Modern NLP relies on pre-trained language models (like GPT, BERT) that learn language patterns from massive text corpora, then fine-tune on specific tasks.

cv.title: Computer Vision
cv.short: Giving machines the ability to see and understand images.
cv.detail: Computer vision uses deep learning (especially CNNs and Vision Transformers) to interpret visual data. Applications include image classification, object detection, facial recognition, medical imaging analysis, and autonomous driving.

tech.heading: Technical Details
tech.p1: This project is a static web page built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework dependencies. The interactive concept cards use simple DOM manipulation for expand/collapse behavior, and the design follows the site's Vercel-inspired system.

next.heading: What's next
next.p1: Future iterations will include animated diagrams showing how data flows through neural networks, interactive parameter-tuning demos, and a cross-referenced glossary of AI terms.
